t.2.47.1: Having reached that tree and performed the evening twilight worship, Rāma, the best of those who give delight, spoke thus to Lakṣmaṇa.
t.2.47.2: Today is the first night we have spent outside the inhabited land, a night without Sumantra; you should not grieve over it.
t.2.47.3: From this day on, we two must keep watch through the nights without growing weary, for Sītā's welfare and safety rest upon us two, O Lakṣmaṇa.
t.2.47.5: But Rāma, accustomed to costly beds, lay down upon the bare earth and spoke these auspicious words to Saumitri.
t.2.47.4: Somehow, O Saumitri, we pass this night; we lie down upon the ground, having spread out a bed of what we ourselves have gathered.
t.2.47.6: Surely, Lakṣmaṇa, the great king sleeps in sorrow today, but Kaikeyī, her desire fulfilled, must be content.
t.2.47.8: Helpless and old, and separated from me as well, what will he do, ruled by desire and fallen under the power of Kaikeyī?
t.2.47.7: For that queen Kaikeyī, for the sake of the kingdom, might she not even deprive the great king of his life once she sees Bharata arrived?
t.2.47.9: Beholding this calamity and the bewilderment of the king's mind, my conviction is that desire alone weighs more heavily than profit and righteousness.
t.2.47.10: For what man, Lakṣmaṇa, even one without wisdom, would cast off for the sake of a woman a son who follows his every wish, as father has cast off me?
t.2.47.11: Happy indeed is Bharata, the son of Kekayī, together with his wife, who alone will enjoy the joyful Kosalas like a supreme king.
t.2.47.13: Whoever abandons wealth and righteousness and follows desire swiftly comes to such ruin, just as King Daśaratha has.
t.2.47.12: For he alone will be the head of the whole kingdom, now that father is far advanced in years and I have taken to the forest.
t.2.47.15: I hope that Kaikeyī, now deluded by the intoxication of her good fortune, will not torment Kausalyā and Sumitrā on my account.
t.2.47.14: I think, gentle one, that Kaikeyī has come for the death of Daśaratha, for my banishment, and for the kingship of Bharata.
t.2.47.16: Let not Queen Sumitrā dwell in sorrow on my account; go back from here to Ayodhyā in good time, Lakṣmaṇa.
t.2.47.17: I alone will go with Sītā to the Daṇḍaka forests; for you shall be the protector of Kausalyā, who is left without a protector.
t.2.47.18: For Kaikeyī, whose deeds are base, might out of hatred commit some wrong; so you must entrust my mother to Bharata, who knows dharma.
t.2.47.19: Surely, Saumitri, in some former birth my mother separated women from their sons, and that is why this too has now befallen her.
t.2.47.20: For Kausalyā has been parted from me, whom she nourished so long and reared with hardship, at the very time when the fruit was due; shame upon me!
t.2.47.21: O Saumitri, may no married woman ever bear a son such as I, who am causing my mother endless grief.
t.2.47.22: I think, Lakṣmaṇa, that the mynah bird is greater in love than I, she whose words are heard: 'O parrot, bite the foot of the enemy!'
t.2.47.24: For my mother Kausalyā, ill-fated indeed, bereft of me, lies stricken with the deepest sorrow, fallen into an ocean of grief.
t.2.47.23: O tamer of foes, what use is a son like me, who does nothing at all to help her, to that grieving, ill-fated woman who is as good as sonless?
t.2.47.26: I am afraid of the fear of adharma and of the other world, O sinless one; therefore, Lakṣmaṇa, I do not have myself consecrated today.
t.2.47.25: For I alone, Lakṣmaṇa, if roused to anger, could overcome Ayodhyā and even the whole earth with my arrows; yet surely valor is to no purpose.
t.2.47.27: Having lamented piteously in this way and much else besides in that lonely place, Rāma, his face filled with tears, sat down in silence in the night.
t.2.47.28: Lakṣmaṇa comforted Rāma, who had fallen silent after lamenting, like a fire whose flames have died away, like an ocean grown still.
t.2.47.29: Surely today, O Rāma, best of those who bear weapons, the city of Ayodhyā, with you departed, is without radiance, like a night from which the moon has gone.
t.2.47.30: It is not fitting, Rāma, that you torment yourself like this; you dishearten Sītā, and me as well, O bull among men.
t.2.47.31: O Rāghava, bereft of you, neither Sītā nor I could live even for a moment, like two fish drawn out of the water.
t.2.47.32: Indeed, without you, O scorcher of foes, I would not wish to see father today, nor Śatrughna, nor Sumitrā, nor even heaven itself.
t.2.47.33: Having heard thus Lakṣmaṇa's excellent and ample words, Rāghava, scorcher of foes, embracing dharma for a very long time, respectfully resolved upon dwelling in the forest for all the years.
